title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were invoked because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, conservative contamination check (10% Mininet holdout produced zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of methodological tradeoffs, determinism provenance, and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps throughput but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that may cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates prior to application. The operational benefit of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study was designed as a paired experiment that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and (if needed) issuing a single repair prompt on the identical candidate. Our contribution is a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived, externally auditable measurement that clarifies when deterministic repair produces measurable gains under a shared‑initial sampling policy.
sections.related_work: Empirical and survey work documents that large language models exhibit factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained agent architectures, and guardrail designs. NetOps prototypes demonstrate feasibility for intent→configuration translation but rarely provide instrumented failure‑rate evaluations under preregistered designs. Architectural proposals recommend combining LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and guarded agentic patterns; red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can change safety outcomes. Our study positions itself within verifier‑assisted mitigation literature by externally measuring the marginal effect of a deterministic GVR pipeline for a fixed model and a fixed single‑draw generator policy, thereby addressing a gap about workload dependence of GVR gains.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and core design. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task (shared_initial semantics), and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The confirmatory analysis was executed by paired_binary_analysis_v1. The task bank comprised 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each), each encoding initial/final states and workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group‑active minima).

Determinism provenance and sampling semantics. The execution bundle records the declared execution configuration and adapter accounting. The explicit model call parameter labeled "temperature" in the recorded model configuration file is null (no per‑call temperature numeric value set). Deterministic shared‑initial semantics in this run were enforced by the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter rather than by inserting an explicit model temperature numeric parameter; adapter accounting in the archived reconciliation artifacts documents hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200, and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}. These audited adapter fields provide the verifiable runtime evidence that a single initial candidate per task was produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. Because determinism was achieved by adapter enforcement, the shared‑initial paired contrast intentionally excludes any marginal benefit obtainable by independent re‑sampling of the generator (a preplanned design trade‑off to isolate the validator+repair marginal effect).

Validators, emulator holdout, and contamination rule. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). As a conservative contamination detector we preregistered a Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). The contamination rule excluded any pair where validator verdict != emulator verdict; in this run the contamination summary reports zero disagreements for the holdout. We note an explicit reproducibility gap: the archived artifact set does not include a labeled selection seed for the randomized Mininet holdout, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout selection even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements. We treat this as a documented limitation rather than a methodological failure.

Execution accounting, repair policy, and inferential plan. The adapter enforced a model‑call budget cap (maximum_model_calls = 400): initial generations = 200 and up to 200 repair calls allowed. The preregistered repair policy issued at most one automated repair prompt when the primary validator reported violations; any repaired candidate would be re‑validated and recorded. The primary statistical test uses the 2×2 paired contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00) with exact McNemar inference; bootstrap percentile CIs quantify paired difference uncertainty. Sensitivity analyses (preplanned) address contamination treatment and missingness handling; they were invoked only when required by flags or failures.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 400 shared across two conditions), produced a complete_pair_count = 200, and consumed model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair_calls_used = 0 because no validator failures occurred. Adapter audit fields (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 200) corroborate the single shared initial invocation semantics.

Validator outcomes and primary inferential result. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed paired difference = 0.0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) equals [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent on this task bank and under the enforced shared‑initial policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated meaningfully.

Repair, secondary outcomes, and contamination check. No repairs were applied; secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) therefore contain no empirical observations in this run. The Mininet 10% holdout contamination detector reported zero disagreements between validator and emulator on the sampled tasks; however, as noted in Methods the explicit holdout selection seed is not labeled in the public artifacts, which limits exact determinism of the holdout reconstruction despite the zero‑disagreement finding.

Representative diagnostics. Representative validator traces for tasks of varying declared difficulty (labels: medium, hard, very_hard) confirm that parsed_command_count matched required_command_count and validation_after.valid = true for sampled examples. These diagnostics show the task bank exercised nontrivial workflow constraints (patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) even though the generator outputs satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints under the chosen generation policy.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The artifact‑grounded null outcome—no validator‑detected failures under the shared‑initial design—does not imply GVR is universally unnecessary. Rather, it precisely indicates that, for this curated task bank and this generator/prompt policy with adapter‑enforced single draws, there were no validator‑detectable errors for GVR to rectify. The marginal value of deterministic repair therefore depends on baseline failure prevalence and on validator coverage for the operational workload.

Why the null occurred. Archived validator traces show that generator outputs consistently included required commands and respected declared workflow constraints; adapter accounting documents single shared initial draws. Together these artifacts explain why no validator failures materialized at scale. The preregistered Mininet holdout produced no validator–emulator disagreements in the sampled tasks, but the missing labeled selection seed for the holdout weakens the reproducibility of that corroboration and is an explicit limitation.

Methodological tradeoffs and guidance. The shared‑initial paired design isolates the causal effect of validation+repair on an identical candidate but excludes benefits obtainable by independent re‑sampling of the generator (multi‑sample policies can increase the chance of observing failing candidates that repairs could correct). Practitioners should therefore choose designs aligned to the operational question: paired shared‑initial contrasts measure marginal guardrail impact on fixed generator draws; independent multi‑sample designs estimate unconditional operational failure rates and unconditional repair utility. When baseline failures are rare under production generator settings, investments in enhancing validator fidelity (richer device semantics, extended emulation) or in adversarial testing may offer more operational risk reduction than a single‑step automated repair.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is supported by preregistration, deterministic adapter enforcement, and reconciliation artifacts confirming episode accounting. Construct validity depends on validator expressiveness—deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces specified syntactic and intent checks but cannot capture all device idiosyncrasies or emergent runtime failure modes. External validity is limited by the single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), the shared_initial deterministic sampling policy, the curated synthetic/public task bank, and the single‑repair budget. Conclusion validity is constrained by zero discordant pairs, which produces an exact but uninformative McNemar test regarding the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction target.

Reproducibility and artifact provenance. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle described in the Disclosure Statement. To address reviewer feedback we have removed raw per‑file JSON snippets and long cryptographic lists from the main text; those low‑level provenance artifacts remain available in the archived execution bundle for auditors. We explicitly document the one reproducibility gap discovered during review research: the randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present among labeled artifacts, preventing exact deterministic reconstruction of that holdout draw and therefore limiting exact replay of the contamination check draw.
sections.conclusion: Under a preregistered paired shared‑initial design on a 200‑task intent→configuration bank, a deterministic GVR pipeline with adapter‑enforced single draws produced no validator‑detectable failures to correct: baseline and guarded conditions both passed the primary deterministic validator on all tasks (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), producing an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded result clarifies that GVR’s marginal benefit is workload‑dependent: when validator‑detectable failures are rare for the chosen generator/prompt policy, a single automated repair pass yields no measured safety gain for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory studies should (i) target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, (ii) consider mixed designs that include independent multi‑sample draws to estimate unconditional failure rates, (iii) expand validator fidelity with larger emulation or selective device checks (and record holdout seeds), and (iv) evaluate multi‑step repair budgets or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation to exercise richer repair pathways. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived with the preregistration id cited in the Disclosure Statement for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure. This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The human Research Director limited the topic family to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes; no human manual editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Frameworks and tools: orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). Execution accounting: the run executed autonomously under the frozen preregistered plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z). Model‑call budget and usage: model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Determinism provenance: the recorded model_configuration lists temperature = null; deterministic shared‑initial semantics were enforced by the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter at runtime and are evidenced by adapter/provider accounting fields in the reconciliation artifacts (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 200; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}). Validation/emulation: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the contamination summary reports zero disagreements for that holdout. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired shared‑initial design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task) was frozen prior to any model calls. All model calls, prompts, adapter accounting fields, validator traces, emulator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the preregistration id for independent inspection.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: results reflect a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); generalization to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions is limited.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) under adapter‑enforced shared_initial generation was tested (adapter accounting documents single shared invocations). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can miss device idiosyncrasies or emergent runtime failure modes detectable only by richer emulation or real devices.
Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks, which prior audits show can bypass naive defenses.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, alternate repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
